newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: El Nino seen hitting quality of Colombia coffee.
newsitem.headline: El Nino seen hitting quality of Colombia coffee.

text.p: Hot weather caused by the El Nino effect could lead to a deterioration in the quality of Colombian coffee in the 1997/98 cycle, experts said Monday.

But the phenomenon, which meteorologists say will bring exceptionally hot, dry spells to part of this Andean nation and unseasonal, torrential rains to other areas, is unlikely to affect the volume of the crop, coffee experts said.

"Until now there's not really been a problem but if the summer continues like this then there could be problems with the quality," Omar Acevedo, technical director of the Coffee Growers' Committee in central Risaralda province, told Reuters.
The beans are currently maturing on trees ahead of the main coffee harvest which is due to begin in September and provides about 60 percent of the country's total crop.
If August is too hot and dry, beans will fail to develop and will begin to dry out -- thereby producing sub-export quality coffee.
In other areas, trees are currently flowering ahead of the smaller so-called Mitaca harvest which begins in about April and provides 40 percent of national output.

Jose Maria Astaiza, technical director with the Cauca province Coffee Committee, said warm, dry weather now will help flowering for the Mitaca crop but if periods of high temperatures are prolonged the flowers could dry and fall prematurely.
Environment Minister Eduardo Verano said the greatest risk of unusually high temperatures is in central and western parts of the country -- precisely around the main coffee growing area.

The area which so far seems to be suffering most from the El Nino effect, caused by a cyclical warming of the Pacific Ocean which then produces freak climate patterns, is Valle de Cauca province in the southwest.
"It's not rained for a month here," said Humberto Vanegas, a technical adviser with the National Coffee Growers' Committee.

He said temperatures had been running in excess of 30 degrees centigrade. Valle de Cauca provides about 10 percent of the national coffee harvest, which is estimated at 12 million 60-kg bags for the 1997/98 coffee year.
